Chapter 8. The Gift of Perspective: Seeing the World with New Eyes
Have you ever noticed how illness can sharpen your senses? Suddenly, colors look brighter, laughter sounds a little louder, and even the tiniest pleasures start to feel important. The things that used to seem urgent—maybe chasing that next promotion, planning the perfect getaway, or worrying about what strangers think—those start to fade into the background. And what takes their place? A whole new way of seeing, grounded in gratitude and being truly present.
Let me tell you about a woman who spent years running after success. One afternoon, she just sat in her backyard, quietly watching her kids play. The sun felt warm on her skin, the air smelled sweet, and for a moment, all her worries just slipped away. That’s when it hit her—happiness isn’t a goal to chase. It’s something you notice, in the middle of ordinary life, right here, right now.
Most of us, we’re always rushing, always looking ahead, always wanting a little bit more. But when the future suddenly seems uncertain, the present moment becomes so precious. Think about it—a shared meal, your favorite song coming on, a quiet evening with people you love. These little things, the ones we often overlook, suddenly become treasures.
Gaining some perspective also helps us see what really matters. Old grudges don’t seem so important anymore, and those petty arguments? They just lose their grip. Forgiveness feels easier. There’s a new urge to make amends, to tell people how much they mean to us, to leave nothing unsaid. And you know what? Being aware of our own mortality doesn’t have to be dark or depressing. In fact, it can light a fire under us—a reminder to live fully, to savor every single day, and to make the most of the time we’ve got.
Of course, shifting your perspective isn’t always easy. There are tough days, when fear or sadness just seem too much, when the sense of loss feels overwhelming. But even then, there’s often a bit of beauty to be found—a kind word, a gentle touch, a real moment of connection.
Over time, you start to realize that maybe the greatest gift of hardship is learning to see the world with fresh eyes. To truly appreciate the ordinary, to find joy in the simple things, and to spot the extraordinary hidden in everyday moments.
That’s the gift that illness, for all its struggles, can give us—a deeper, fuller, more meaningful life.
